query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐solidification aging treatment that promotes the formation of fine, coherent nanoprecipitates within the lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure of a eutectic HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will simultaneously enhance both strength and ductility relative to the as‐cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a lamellar fcc/B2 dual-phase structure (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) exhibiting a balance of moderate strength and ductility.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored aging heat treatment at an optimized temperature and time to induce controlled coherent nanoprecipitation within one of the lamellar phases.
generation.conditions: Under processing conditions typical for structural applications—aging performed at a temperature low enough to preserve the lamellar architecture (e.g., between 400–600°C) and for durations calibrated to obtain a uniform, nanoscale precipitate distribution without coarsening, tested at room temperature and moderate service temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform distribution of fine, coherent nanoprecipitates (for example, NiAl-rich particles) that remain embedded within the ductile fcc phase while maintaining an optimal interlamellar spacing.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion (thereby increasing strength) while the coherent interfaces help relieve local stress concentrations and promote dislocation transmission across the lamellae (thus preserving or even enhancing ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in yield strength and ultimate tensile strength accompanied by improved ductility (higher elongation) relative to the untreated as‐cast eutectic HEA.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) without any additional aging treatment.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected as long as the aging treatment is carefully controlled to avoid overaging or precipitate coarsening; if the coherent interface integrity is lost or the lamellar structure is disrupted, the improvements may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal aging temperature and time window are not known a priori and must be determined experimentally; additionally, the precise quantitative enhancements in strength and ductility are uncertain pending experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of samples of the eutectic HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with one group kept in the as‐cast condition and other groups subjected to aging treatments at several temperatures (e.g., 400°C, 500°C, 600°C) and varying durations. After processing, perform tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation, and conduct microscopic analyses (TEM and XRD) to assess the size, distribution, and coherence of the nanoprecipitates as well as the integrity of the lamellar microstructure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the aging treatment conditions yield a simultaneous and statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as‐cast state, or if the aging treatment leads to precipitate coarsening and loss of coherence resulting in embrittlement, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
